sections.heading: Coming to you with what I lack
sections.text:
Lord Jesus, I come to you as I really am. I do not see clearly, so be my light. I do not have the wisdom I need, so teach me. My will bends toward myself, so reshape my thoughts and desires until they move with yours.

Help me hear the Spirit’s voice quickly and gladly. Make me ready to follow when he leads. Keep my conscience soft and awake, so that I do not make peace with even the smallest evil.
theological_themes: Human weakness and dependence on Christ

scripture_references.connection: Jesus identifies himself as the light of the world, which grounds the prayer’s request for him to lead a spiritually needy person out of darkness and into true life.
James directs believers who lack wisdom to ask God for it. This supports the prayer’s honest confession of ignorance and dependence on God’s generous instruction.
Jesus teaches that the Spirit guides his people into truth. The prayer’s desire to hear and follow the Spirit rests on this promised ministry.

sections.heading: Running to Christ when fear and accusation come
sections.text:
When the enemy comes near with accusations, fear, or temptation, teach me to run straight to your wounds. Let the cross be the place where my panic quiets, because there my sin has already been dealt with.

Be my good Shepherd. Lead me into the living fields of your Word, and let me rest beside the steady waters of your comfort. Fill me with your peace, so that the winds of this world do not keep stirring up my soul.
theological_themes: Refuge in Christ’s wounds and cross

scripture_references.connection: Peter connects Christ’s wounds with the healing of sinners and immediately speaks of returning to the Shepherd and Overseer of the soul. This closely supports both fleeing to Christ’s wounds and trusting him as Shepherd.
Jesus calls himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, grounding the prayer’s confidence that his care is secured by his sacrifice.
Paul teaches that God’s peace guards believers as they bring their anxieties to him. This supports the request for a soul kept calm amid worldly trouble.

sections.heading: Resting in what your cross has done
sections.text:
Your cross stands as my refuge. Your blood cleanses me. Your death is the guarantee that I am not left to answer for myself. Your name is the only name I can plead, and it is enough to save me.

Through you, heaven has already begun to be poured into my heart, but my heart is too small to take in the greatness of your love.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says redemption and forgiveness come through Christ’s blood, which directly grounds the prayer’s confidence that Jesus’ blood cleanses and saves.
Hebrews presents Jesus as the guarantor of a better covenant and the living intercessor who saves completely. This supports the prayer’s language of Christ as the sure guarantee before God.
The apostles proclaim that salvation is found in no other name than Jesus. This supports the prayer’s trust in Christ’s name as the only sufficient plea.
Paul prays that believers would know Christ’s love even though it surpasses knowledge. This captures the prayer’s sense that Christ’s love fills the heart while exceeding its capacity.

sections.heading: Remembering what you have made me
sections.text: I was far off from you — a stranger, an outsider, a slave, and a rebel. But by your cross you brought me near. You softened my hard heart. You made me your Father’s child. You gave me a place in your family. You joined me to yourself so that what is yours by grace becomes mine too.
theological_themes: Alienation from God apart from Christ

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes Gentile believers as once alienated and far off, then brought near by the blood of Christ and made members of God’s household. This strongly supports the movement from outcast to family member.
Paul teaches that believers receive the Spirit of adoption, cry to God as Father, and become heirs with Christ. This grounds the prayer’s language of sonship, family, and shared inheritance.
Galatians connects Christ’s redeeming work with adoption and heirship. It supports the prayer’s claim that former slaves are made children and heirs through Jesus.

sections.heading: Asking to love you and become like you
sections.text:
Lord Jesus, let me love you because you first loved me. Help me live in a way that fits the mercy you have shown me. Make my life reflect you, the firstborn over your new creation and the true image of God.

Keep my eyes of faith clear so I can keep seeing your beauty. Let me know the strong, living work of your Spirit in my heart, because unless he moves in me with power, no real fire for you will burn there.
theological_themes: Love as a response to Christ’s love
Dependence on the Spirit for spiritual life

scripture_references.connection: John teaches that Christian love is a response to God’s prior love. This supports the prayer’s desire to love Christ as one already loved by him.
Paul prays that believers would walk in a manner worthy of the Lord and bear fruit. This directly supports the request for a life that fits Christ’s mercy.
Paul describes believers beholding the Lord’s glory and being transformed into his image by the Spirit. This grounds the prayer’s longing to see Christ’s beauty and be made like him.
Paul prays for believers to be strengthened with power through the Spirit in the inner person. This supports the prayer’s dependence on the Spirit for inward spiritual fire and strength.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses strong spiritual-warfare language about Satan approaching. I kept that as real personal opposition through accusation, fear, and temptation without expanding it beyond the prayer’s focus on fleeing to Christ.

The phrase about Christ’s name being the believer’s “property” can sound possessive or transactional in modern English. I rendered it as the only name the believer can plead and trust for salvation, preserving the idea of Christ given to the believer without implying control over him.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Be thou my mind” was rendered as Christ reshaping the person’s thoughts and desires, rather than replacing the person’s agency. This preserves the request for inward submission to Christ while avoiding an unnatural or misleading modern phrasing.

“Thy death occurred to give me a surety” was interpreted in light of Christ as covenant guarantor and intercessor, so the modern prayer says his death is the guarantee that I am not left to answer for myself.

“By thee all heaven is poured into my heart” was rendered as heaven already beginning to be poured into the heart through Christ. This keeps the experiential richness while avoiding the implication that the believer already possesses the fullness of heaven in this life.
